LOS ANGELES, California (CNN) — He is the global star who brought the legendary comic-book character Wolverine to the screen. Her films, including the full “X-Men” series, have taken in more than $2 billion around the world.

Hugh Jackman appears as Wolverine in “X-Men Origins: Wolverine,” which debuted Friday.

Jackman and producer Lauren Shuler Donner recently had an open discussion about their new movie, “X-Men Origins: Wolverine.” They focused in particular on the sequence where Jackman’s character changes from an ordinary mutant whose bone claws occasionally extend from the backs of his hands into a seemingly unstoppable mutant infused with adamantium, an unbreakable metal. The moment marks the true creation of a comic-book icon, as Logan becomes Wolverine.

Jackman said he understood that this was the character’s defining origin moment — the point where audiences finally see him fully unleashed. In the comics, he explained, it is known as “berserker rage.” Although the phrase is not really part of standard English, he joked that it might be now. For him, the scene captured the idea of a completely wild creature being set free, which ties into the larger story: the conflict between the animal side and the human side, something he believes everyone can recognize.

Donner said the tank sequence required Jackman to perform several difficult actions. He had to be lowered into the tank, and then the needles had to move toward him. Since most of the needles were computer-generated, he had to react by looking at specific spots where they would later appear. The problem was that he could not hear director Gavin Hood. The crew experimented with different noises, speakers and other methods before finally creating a system using Jackman’s toes. If Hood pulled on Jackman’s big toe, it meant the needles were coming; another toe meant something else; and the final toe signal meant he should rise up. Donner jokingly described the system as “very sophisticated.”

Jackman said he had decided that he needed to be in far more extreme physical condition for the scene — not simply fitter, but shaped in a different, almost absurd way — because he wanted the transformation to feel unsettling. He wanted viewers to have the same reaction he had when watching Robert De Niro in “Cape Fear”: the sense that the character was powerful, threatening, dangerous and capable of exploding at any moment.

Donner added that the filmmakers were aiming to recreate a famous comic-book image of Wolverine bursting out of the tank, enraged, with things protruding from his body and his hair wild around him. That was the visual they wanted to deliver for fans.

Jackman admitted that when he saw the finished scene, it unnerved him a little. He found himself wondering whether that was really him. His wife, Deb, reacted similarly, telling him that it was ridiculous and that she did not even recognize the person on screen.

**“CLAWS OUT: REVISITING WOLVERINE’S BEGINNING”**  
*A transcript-style movie feature — Los Angeles*

**INT. PRIVATE SCREENING ROOM — LOS ANGELES — LATE AFTERNOON**

A low amber wash of California light leaks through the edges of blackout curtains. On the screen: a paused frame of a young James Howlett, trembling in a nightshirt, bone claws newly erupted from his hands.

HUGH JACKMAN sits forward in his chair, elbows on knees, looking at the image with the half-smile of someone seeing both a character and an old scar.

Beside him, producer LAUREN SHULER DONNER folds her hands, watching the frame quietly.

A small crew adjusts microphones. Coffee cups sit on the table. Outside, Los Angeles traffic murmurs like static.

---

**INTERVIEWER:**  
When people talk about Wolverine, they usually talk about the claws, the attitude, the cigar, the one-liners. But his origin is traumatic. It’s a child discovering violence in himself. How did you approach that?

**HUGH JACKMAN:**  
That was always the key for me. Wolverine isn’t cool because he has claws. He’s compelling because the claws cost him something. The origin scene is not a superhero moment. It’s a horror moment. It’s a boy’s body betraying him, or at least that’s how it feels to him.

He doesn’t understand what’s happening. There’s grief, fear, rage — all arriving at once. And then suddenly the body becomes a weapon.

**LAUREN SHULER DONNER:**  
Exactly. We never wanted it to feel like, “Here comes Wolverine.” It had to feel like, “This is where James ends.” The persona comes much later. The swagger, the armor, the sarcasm — all of that is built over a wound.

**HUGH JACKMAN:**  
Logan is someone who spends a lifetime trying not to feel that first moment again.

---

**CUT TO: ARCHIVAL FOOTAGE — SET PHOTOS AND STORYBOARDS**

Pencil sketches of claws emerging from small fists. Notes about lighting. A bedroom set. Snow outside a window. Blood on floorboards.

---

**INTERVIEWER:**  
Lauren, as a producer, how do you balance the comic-book mythology with something that emotionally raw?

**LAUREN SHULER DONNER:**  
You respect both. The mythology matters because fans know what that moment means. But if you only serve the mythology, it becomes a checklist: claws, scream, tragedy. The emotion is what makes it cinema.

We talked a lot about innocence. That scene had to be about a child who cannot go back to being a child. The audience may know the legend of Wolverine, but the boy in that room does not.

**HUGH JACKMAN:**  
And that’s the tragedy. He’s not choosing a destiny. It’s erupting out of him.

---

**INTERVIEWER:**  
The “berserker rage” is such a defining part of Wolverine. It can look exciting on screen, but it’s also terrifying. How did you think about that state?

**HUGH JACKMAN:**  
I never thought of it as anger in the simple sense. It’s not, “I’m annoyed, so I’m going to lash out.” Berserker rage is what happens when every restraint is gone. It’s animal survival. It’s grief without language.

For me, physically, it was about stripping away control. Logan is incredibly controlled most of the time — even when he seems rough. He’s always holding something back. The berserker rage is the moment the dam breaks.

**LAUREN SHULER DONNER:**  
And Hugh understood that it couldn’t just be choreography. It had to feel dangerous, even to Logan. Especially to Logan.

**HUGH JACKMAN:**  
Yeah. If he’s comfortable in it, it’s not rage. It’s a superpower trick. But the point is that it costs him. He wakes up from those moments with the emotional equivalent of blood on his hands, whether literal or not.

---

**INT. SCREENING ROOM — CONTINUOUS**

The scene on the monitor rolls briefly: the young boy runs, shocked and horrified. The room watches in silence.

---

**INTERVIEWER:**  
Did you ever worry that audiences would enjoy the berserker rage too much?

**LAUREN SHULER DONNER:**  
Of course. That’s always the tension with Wolverine. He’s thrilling. He’s primal. There’s a reason audiences respond to him. But our responsibility was to never let the violence become weightless.

**HUGH JACKMAN:**  
The claws are satisfying in an action scene, no question. But if you forget they came from pain, you lose the character.

What I loved about Logan from the start is that he’s ashamed of the thing everyone else thinks is cool. People look at him and say, “That’s incredible.” He’s thinking, “You have no idea.”

---

**INTERVIEWER:**  
How much of Wolverine’s rage comes from fear?

**HUGH JACKMAN:**  
A huge amount. Rage is often fear with armor on. Logan is terrified of loss, terrified of attachment, terrified of himself. His whole life is this question: “If I get close to you, will I hurt you? Will I fail you? Will I outlive you?”

The berserker side is the part of him that says, “Don’t think. Don’t feel. Survive.” But the man underneath wants connection desperately.

**LAUREN SHULER DONNER:**  
That’s why he works. He’s not just a loner because it looks cool in a leather jacket. He’s a loner because intimacy is dangerous to him.

---

**CUT TO: BEHIND-THE-SCENES STYLE INSERT**

A stunt coordinator demonstrates claw movements. Jackman rehearses with tense shoulders, jaw clenched, breath heavy. The movements are not elegant. They are abrupt, brutal, almost unwilling.

---

**INTERVIEWER:**  
Hugh, did you have a physical trigger for getting into that berserker state?

**HUGH JACKMAN:**  
Breath. Always breath. I would change the breathing first. Shallow, fast, almost like the body is preparing for impact. Then the shoulders come up, the neck tightens, the eyes narrow — not in a “movie tough guy” way, but like an animal trying to locate the threat.

The trick was not to play rage as loud all the time. Sometimes the scariest moment is just before. The stillness. Logan deciding — or maybe failing to decide — whether he can stop himself.

**LAUREN SHULER DONNER:**  
That stillness was important. Hugh could communicate the fight before the fight. The battle inside him was always more interesting than the external one.

---

**INTERVIEWER:**  
The origin scene also deals with identity: James Howlett, Logan, Wolverine. How did you see those names?

**HUGH JACKMAN:**  
James is the boy. Logan is the man trying to function. Wolverine is what the world calls the monster, and eventually what he learns to carry.

But I never wanted to play them as separate people exactly. They’re layers. In the rage, you see the oldest layer — the frightened child — and the most primal layer — the animal — at the same time.

**LAUREN SHULER DONNER:**  
That’s beautifully put. The origin isn’t just an explanation of powers. It’s the first fracture.

---

**INT. SCREENING ROOM — DUSK**

Los Angeles has turned blue beyond the curtains. The paused image on the screen glows colder now.

---

**INTERVIEWER:**  
Looking back, why do you think that origin still matters to audiences?

**LAUREN SHULER DONNER:**  
Because everyone understands the fear of something inside you that you can’t control. Maybe not claws, obviously, but anger, grief, trauma, instinct. Wolverine externalizes that. He makes it mythic.

**HUGH JACKMAN:**  
And because he keeps trying. That’s the part people sometimes miss. The rage is iconic, but the heroism is in the restraint. It’s in the fact that he has every excuse to become the monster people say he is — and he fights, again and again, not to.

**INTERVIEWER:**  
So the berserker rage is not the essence of Wolverine?

**HUGH JACKMAN:**  
No. The essence is what happens after. The guilt. The choice. The effort to be better.

A beat.

**HUGH JACKMAN:**  
The rage is the wound speaking. Logan is the man trying to answer it.

Lauren nods, eyes still on the screen.

**LAUREN SHULER DONNER:**  
That’s why he endures. Not because he can heal from anything physically. Because emotionally, he shouldn’t be able to — and yet he keeps going.

---

**FADE OUT.**
